1:
“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.” The witnesses open the New Testament with the human genealogy of Christ, and dwell on its title and its theological weight. The Latin fathers, with Jerome, note that Matthew, signified by “the face of a man” in Ezekiel’s vision, fitly “opens his Gospel with the human genealogy of Christ,” and that Isaiah’s “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8) speaks of the divine generation, not contradicted here. Ambrose marks the naming of “two authors of His birth” — David and Abraham — the heads of the kingly and the covenant lines. The grammatical-historical commentators attend to the words: Robertson notes “the Book” (biblos, our “Bible”), and Henry that “the book of the generation” (biblos geneseōs) is the Hebrew manner of titling a narrative of descent. Lightfoot supplies the Jewish background of carefully kept genealogies.

The deepest stress falls on the person of the One whose genealogy this is. The Eastern Chrysostom calls the title “the sum of the whole dispensation, the root of all its blessings — that God became man.” Against the heresies that made Christ a mere man — Cerinthus, Ebion, Paul of Samosata (Augustine) — the Eastern Alexandrian voices set his eternal deity: Pseudo-Athanasius cites “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), and Cyril of Alexandria, “who being in the form of God thought it not robbery to be equal with God” (Philippians 2:6). Cyril of Jerusalem holds both together: “the Son of David at the end of the ages, but the Son of God before all ages.” Calvin, for the Reformed, opens the much-debated question whether Matthew and Luke both trace the line through Joseph, or Matthew through Joseph and Luke through Mary. The witnesses thus find in the opening verse the great theme of the Gospel: the eternal Son of God, true God before all ages, has become true man, the son of David and of Abraham, entering the human line to fulfil the promises made to the fathers — his genealogy according to the flesh the seal of a real incarnation.
2:
“Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren.” The witnesses note the chosen line and the names passed over. The grammatical-historical commentators explain that only the direct line of promise is traced: Robertson observes that “begat” (egennēsen) runs with regularity to v.16, where the form changes at the birth of Jesus, and that it “does not always mean immediate parentage, but direct descent.” Gill, Clarke, and Ellicott note why Ishmael and Esau are omitted — they were “outside the covenant,” for “in Isaac shall thy seed be called” (Genesis 21:12), and Esau “had forfeited both the birthright and the blessing.” Yet “Judah and his brethren” are all named, the twelve patriarchs being together the people of God.

The fathers read the names mystically. The Latin Ambrose marks Abraham as “the first who deserved the witness of faith,” who “believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). The Eastern Pseudo-Chrysostom finds Christ figured in the names: Isaac, “laughter,” the joy of the heart; Jacob, “supplanter”; Judah, “confessor,” a type of Christ who confessed the Father (Matthew 11:25). Calvin, for the Reformed, notes that the twelve patriarchs are all given a place, “on all of whom God had bestowed a similar favour of adoption,” the blessing extending to the whole chosen people, not Judah alone. The witnesses thus find in the verse both history and grace. The genealogy follows not the firstborn by nature but the line of promise, chosen by God’s free election — Isaac not Ishmael, Jacob not Esau — so that from the first the descent of Christ is marked by sovereign grace. And the naming of “Judah and his brethren” shows that, though the Messiah springs from Judah alone, the whole house of Israel is gathered into the covenant story that leads to him.

The witnesses observe that the genealogy thus begins where the promises began. From Abraham, to whom it was said ‘in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed,’ the line of blessing runs through the chosen sons to Christ, in whom the promise is fulfilled. The verse therefore is no dry list but the tracing of a covenant: each ‘begat’ carries forward the pledge made to the fathers, until the Seed should come in whom all nations are blessed. The reader is taught to see, in the bare succession of names, the patient faithfulness of God keeping his word across the generations.
3:
“And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar; and Phares begat Esrom; and Esrom begat Aram.” The witnesses note especially the naming of Tamar, the first of the women in the genealogy. The Latin fathers dwell on the surprise of it: Jerome observes that “none of the holy women are taken into the Saviour’s genealogy, but rather such as Scripture has condemned,” so that “He who came for sinners being born of sinners might put away the sins of all.” Ambrose contrasts Matthew with Luke, who “avoided the mention of these, that he might set forth the series of the priestly race immaculate,” while Matthew’s plan did not exclude “the righteousness of natural reason.” The grammatical-historical commentators supply the history: the Gloss notes that Judah “begat Phares and Zarah before he went into Egypt,” and the line runs on through Esrom and Aram (cf. Genesis 38:29; Ruth 4:18).

The witnesses dwell on the grace displayed in the women’s names. The genealogy of the holy Saviour includes Tamar, whose union with Judah was shameful, as later it will name Rahab the harlot, Ruth the Moabitess, and the wife of Uriah — none of them chosen for their honour, several of them Gentiles or sinners. The fathers and the commentators alike read in this a deliberate design: that the Messiah, who came to save sinners, should spring from a line that included sinners and strangers, so that his very pedigree preaches the gospel of grace. The witnesses thus find in the mention of Tamar a quiet but striking testimony. The Evangelist does not hide the stains in Christ’s ancestry but records them, that the reader may see from the outset that the Saviour entered a fallen race not as one ashamed of it, but as one who came to redeem it. The women whom Scripture had marked with shame are taken up into the lineage of the sinless One, foreshadowing the mercy by which he would gather sinners and Gentiles into the family of God.

The witnesses add that the inclusion of Tamar guards the genealogy from every boast of human merit. Had the line been adorned only with the names of the great and the holy, men might have thought the Saviour came of a worthy stock; but the naming of the shameful teaches that he came of grace alone, stooping to a race of sinners. So the verse, in a single name, overturns all pride of ancestry and prepares the reader for a Christ who is the friend of sinners, born among them that he might save them.
4: “And Aram begat Aminadab; and Aminadab begat Naasson; and Naasson begat Salmon.” Of these three names the commentators dwell on Naasson. Ellicott identifies him as Nahshon, “the brother of Elisheba the wife of Aaron,” who at the time of the Exodus was “prince (or captain) of the children” of Judah (Numbers 1:7; 1 Chronicles 2:10), and adds that a Jewish legend made him the first to enter the waters of the Red Sea. Wesley sets the same man at the other end of the wilderness years, prince of the tribe of Judah “when the Israelites entered into Canaan.” Gill’s remark is on the record rather than the man: the succession here, with what follows in the verse, “exactly agrees with the genealogical account” of the older Scriptures, so that the Evangelist and the registers may be laid side by side without discrepancy. The line of promise thus runs, in this generation, through the house that stood at the head of Judah both in the desert and at the entry into the land; and with Salmon, the last name in the verse, it reaches the generation of the conquest.
5:
“And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse.” Two more women enter the list, and both are outsiders. The grammatical-historical commentators mark the surprise of “Rachab”: Gill observes that, while the older Scriptures say Salmon begat Boaz (Ruth 4:21), it is the Evangelist who tells us his mother was “Rahab, that is, Rahab the harlot” of Jericho (Joshua 6:25). Then follows “Obed of Ruth” — the Moabite widow of the book that bears her name (Ruth 4:13).

Ellicott dwells on that first marriage, of which the earlier records say nothing: the fact was “probably thought of as a blot rather than a glory” when they were compiled, though it may have been kept in the traditions of the house of David. He reports the conjecture that Salmon was himself one of the two unnamed spies whose lives Rahab saved, doing the work Caleb had done before him, and notes that her fame had risen by the time the Gospel was written, as the citations of her elsewhere show (James 2:25; Hebrews 11:31). Salmon, he adds, seems to have been the first of his house to hold land at Bethlehem (1 Chronicles 2:54), gaining it partly through adoption into the family of Caleb. On Ellicott’s reading this new fact lights up much in the later story: the readiness with which the sons of Naomi marry two women of the Moabites, the absence of any repugnance to such a union on the part of Boaz, perhaps even the reference to Tamar in the benediction pronounced upon Ruth (Ruth 4:12).

Gill and Lightfoot trace what the rabbis made of Rahab. So far they agree with the Evangelist, Lightfoot says, that they confess she was married to some prince of Israel, “but mistaking concerning the person” — several naming Joshua. The Babylonian Gemara reckons eight prophets and priests sprung from her, Neriah, Baruch, Seraiah, Maaseiah, Jeremiah, Hilkiah, Hanameel and Shallum, with R. Judah adding Huldah the prophetess; Ellicott remarks that the legend, curiously, includes none of the line of David. The Gloss raises a scruple against the marriage with Joshua, since union with Canaanite proselytes was forbidden, and answers it two ways: either she was not of the seven nations but sojourned among them, or the prohibition did not take effect before the entry into the promised land. Gill cuts through the accretions — “the truth of the matter is, she became the wife of Salmon” — and Wesley closes with a note of providence, that Salmon, Boaz and Obed must each have been near a hundred years old at the birth of the son here recorded.
6:
“And Jesse begat David the king; and David the king begat Solomon of her that had been the wife of Urias.” The witnesses note the royal title given to David and the veiled naming of Bathsheba. The Latin fathers dwell on the latter: Remigius asks why Matthew does not name Bathsheba as he named the other women, and answers that the others, “though deserving of much blame, were yet commendable for many virtues,” while she shared in the great sin; the Gloss adds that, by naming “Urias” instead, the Evangelist “recalls to memory that great wickedness.” Ambrose praises David, who “confessed himself to be but man” and washed out his sin “with the tears of repentance.” Augustine reads the descent through Solomon as fitting Matthew’s theme of Christ “taking on him our sins,” David having sinned in Solomon’s mother.

The grammatical-historical and Reformed commentators note the emphatic “the king.” Calvin observes that “the designation of king is bestowed on David alone, because in his person God exhibited a type of the future leader of his people, the Messiah”; Wesley agrees it is given “because his throne is given to the Messiah” (cf. Luke 1:32). Gill notes that David, “the youngest of Jesse’s sons… despised by his brethren,” was chosen and anointed by God. The witnesses thus find in the verse the meeting of royalty and grace. The genealogy reaches its kingly height in David, the type of Christ the King, whose throne the Messiah would inherit for ever; yet at that very height it records the darkest stain — the sin with the wife of Uriah — naming the wronged husband to keep the guilt in view. The witnesses read in this both warning and comfort: the royal line of the Saviour passes through a repentant sinner, so that the King who comes of David’s house is shown to be the King who saves sinners, of whom David, fallen and forgiven, is at once the ancestor and the type.

The witnesses dwell further on the union of majesty and mercy in this verse. The genealogy reaches its royal summit in David the king, yet at that summit it records his deepest fall; the throne destined for the Messiah is reached through a path of sin and repentance. So the verse holds together the two things the gospel joins: that Christ is the King of David’s line, and that he is the Saviour of David’s kind — sinners who, like David, are restored by grace. The crown and the confession stand side by side, and the King who comes of this house comes to forgive.
7:
“And Solomon begat Roboam; and Roboam begat Abia; and Abia begat Asa; and Asa begat Josaphat; and Josaphat begat Joram; and Joram begat Ozias.” The grammatical-historical commentators supply what is known of these reigns. Gill names the mothers — Roboam born of Naamah an Ammonitess (1 Kings 14:21), Josaphat of Azubah the daughter of Shilhi — and reckons Jehoshaphat “a very good prince.” The harder matter is the gap. Between Joram and Ozias, Lightfoot observes, “the names of Ahazias, Joash, and Amazias are struck out” (1 Chronicles 3:11–12), so that Ozias — the Uzziah struck with leprosy for his presumption in entering the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16) — is Joram’s descendant and not his son. Clarke adds that such omissions “are not uncommon in the Jewish genealogies,” instancing Azariah called the son of Meraioth with six descendants between them, and holds that the Evangelist took the public rolls as he found them, his argument needing no more than an unbroken descent from David. Wesley puts it shortly: Joram begat Uzziah “mediately, as Christ is mediately the son of David and of Abraham.”

The Latin fathers ask not how but why. Jerome sets out the true succession from the fourth book of Kings — Ochozias the son of Joram; then Joash, whom Josabeth hid from the slaughter of the royal seed by Athalias; then Amasias; then Azarias who is called Ozias — and gives two grounds for the silence: the purpose “to make each of the three periods consist of fourteen generations,” and the fact that “Joram had connected himself with Jezebel’s most impious race.” Hilary states the result: “the stain of the Gentile alliance being purged, the royal race is again taken up in the fourth following generation.” The Eastern Pseudo-Chrysostom presses that judgment harder. As Jehu was promised that his children to the fourth generation should sit on the throne of Israel, so a curse of equal reach fell on the house of Joram for the sake of the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, that his sons to the fourth generation “should be cut out of the number of the Kings” — a visiting of the sins of the fathers upon the children (Exodus 20:5), and a warning how dangerous it is to marry with the seed of the ungodly. Augustine proposes another ground: the three were excluded “because their wickedness was continuous and without interval,” where Solomon was suffered to hold the kingdom for his father’s deserts and Roboam for his son’s. Lightfoot notes besides that Joash and Amazias were “sometimes not very unlike Joram in their manners,” and that their kingdom was much eclipsed by the kingdom of Israel.

Beneath the history the fathers trace a moral ascent in the names themselves. Solomon is “peaceful,” the man in whom unlawful motions are composed; Roboam “the breadth of the people,” who looks abroad to draw others with him; Abias “the Lord Father”; Asa “raising up,” who ascends from virtue to virtue; Josaphat “judging”; Joram “lofty,” as dwelling on high; Ozias “the strong One of the Lord,” attributing all his strength to God. Remigius turns the same names upon Christ — our peace, the one Father who is in heaven, he who taketh away the sins of the world, the Son to whom the Father hath committed all judgment (John 5:22) — so that the roll of the kings is read as a catalogue of his titles.
9:
“And Ozias begat Joatham; and Joatham begat Achaz; and Achaz begat Ezekias; and Ezekias begat Manasses; and Manasses begat Amon; and Amon begat Josias.” The grammatical-historical commentators use this stretch of the list to settle what the word “begat” is doing. Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown both begin by identifying the first name: Ozias “is, of course, the Uzziah of the Old Testament,” and three names stand omitted between Joram and him — Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah (1 Chronicles 3:11–12). From that omission Ellicott draws the inference that governs the whole genealogy: “the words ‘A begat B’ are not to be taken literally, but are simply an expression of the fact of succession with or without intermediate links.”

Why these three, and not others, were passed over is disputed. Ellicott judges the motive to have been “simply the desire of bringing the names in each period into which the genealogy is divided to the arbitrary standard of fourteen” — and adds, more tentatively, that since three had in any case to go, the choice may have fallen on these because they belonged to the time of Athaliah’s disastrous influence in the history of the monarchy of Judah. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown grants the first point, that “some omissions behooved to be made, to compress the whole into three fourteens” (v.17), but holds that the particular choice “must be sought in religious considerations,” and lays out three: the connection of those kings with the house of Ahab, as Lightfoot, Ebrard, and Alford view it; their slender right to be reckoned true links in the theocratic chain, as Lange takes it; or some similar disqualification. The three readings agree in this much — that the list is shaped, and that its shape is deliberate rather than careless.

Of the kings named here the commentators record the household facts. Gill notes that Joatham, called Jotham, was born to Ozias of Jerushah the daughter of Zadok, and that Ezekias begat Manasses of Hephzibah. On Manasses his verdict is finely balanced, holding both halves of that reign together: he “was very remarkable both for his sins, and for his humiliation on account of them.” So the line runs on from Manasses through Amon to Josias, and the second of the three fourteens draws toward its close with the captivity now in view — the principle Ellicott drew from the head of the passage governing its end as well, that a name set beside a name in this list asserts succession, and does not always assert fatherhood.
11:
“And Josias begat Jechonias and his brethren, about the time they were carried away to Babylon.” No verse in the genealogy is more contested. Clarke counts three considerable difficulties and adds a fourth: Josias was not the father of Jechonias but his grandfather (1 Chronicles 3:14–16); Jechonias had no brethren on record; Josias died twenty years before the captivity, so that neither he nor they could have been begotten about the time of the deportation; and this second class yields only thirteen names, making forty-one in all where the reckoning requires forty-two. Gill identifies the man at the head of the trouble: Jechonias here is Jehoiakim, whose name before was Eliakim until Pharaohnecho made him king, born to Josias of Zebudah the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah.

On the remedy the commentators divide. Clarke would adopt a reading found in many manuscripts — “Josias begat Joakim, and Joakim begat Jechonias” — by which, he says, every difficulty disappears and the three classes of fourteen stand complete; and he distinguishes accordingly three deportations, the first in the fourth year of Joakim when Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem, the second under Jechonias, who reigned three months before being carried to Babylon with the nobility, the third under Zedekiah. Ellicott will not have it: the marginal reading “rests on very slight authority, and was obviously the insertion of some later scribe, to meet the difficulty.” He grants the missing link in Eliakim, the son of Josiah (2 Kings 23:34), so that Jeconiah is the grandson, and takes “brethren” to cover Mattaniah or Zedekiah, the last king of Judah — Josiah’s son, and so his grandson’s uncle. Wesley answers both questions in a line: begotten “mediately, Jehoiakim coming between,” the brethren being “his uncles,” since the Jews term all kinsmen brethren; and the carrying away followed “a little after the birth of Jeconiah.”

Lightfoot turns to the rabbis for the same knot. The sons of Josias were Jochanan the firstborn, Joachim, Zedekiah, and Shallum, and who this last was the Jerusalem Talmudists dispute: one authority makes Jochanan and Jehoachaz one man, “firstborn to the kingdom” meaning first to reign, and Shallum one with Zedekias, third in birth but fourth in reigning. Lightfoot prefers R. Kimchi “much more correctly”: Shallum is Jechonias, “who had two names, and was reckoned for the son of Josias, when he was his grandchild — for the sons of sons are reputed for sons,” a rule which he thinks the passage itself proclaims (Jeremiah 22:11). So the Evangelist’s two hard words, the fathering and the brethren, are answered from the same usage: descent reckoned by dignity rather than by birth, and kinship named broadly.
12:
“And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel; and Zorobabel begat Abiud… and Matthan begat Jacob.” With the captivity the estate of the house changes. Calvin marks the reversal plainly: “the descendants of David, from being kings, then became exiles and slaves,” and that captivity was “a sort of destruction”; yet it was so ordered that the nation was gathered again and “some vestiges of dominion remained in the family of David,” those who returned submitting of their own accord to Zorobabel, so that the fragments of the royal sceptre lasted until the coming of Christ, according to the word that the sceptre should not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10). Clarke insists the word rendered “carrying away” is better given as transportation, “for the change was not voluntary; they were forced away,” and tells how Jechonias, thirty-seven years in prison, was brought out by Evilmerodach and seated above the kings in Babylon, yet never restored to his kingdom.

That reign never restored raises the chief difficulty of the passage. Jeremiah had said that none of Jeconiah’s seed should sit upon the throne of David; Ambrose answers that the prophet does not declare there shall be no seed at all, and that Christ’s reigning is no contradiction, since “He did not reign with worldly honours” — “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown reads the oracle the same way: “he was to have seed, but no reigning child.” Lightfoot takes “begat” here as succession in dignity rather than in nature — Salathiel “a son of the kingdom,” the honour withered in the rest of Josiah’s sons and somewhat flourishing again in him (2 Kings 25:27) — which is why the Evangelist names Jechonias only. Ellicott sets out the tangle, with Salathiel called the son of Neri in the third Gospel and the son of Assir in the registers, and proposes that Assir died childless before his father, the line of Solomon so failing and the descendants of Nathan taking their place as by adoption. The Gloss is blunter: many parts of the chronicles “have been corrupted by time, and error of transcribers,” whence the controverted questions of genealogies the Apostle bids us avoid (1 Timothy 1:4).

From Abiud onward the names stand outside the canonical records. Gill observes that the sons of Zorobabel named in the registers are Meshullam, Hananiah, and Shelomith their sister, with no mention of Abiud, who “seems to be the same with Meshullam the eldest son, who might have two names” — a thing usual about the time of the captivity, as with Daniel. The Gloss accounts for the Evangelist’s knowledge by other annals, called the Words of the Days, of which much was burned by Herod, a foreigner, “in order to confound the descent of the royal line”; perhaps Joseph had read his ancestors’ names there. The Latin fathers then take the bare names and make them speak. Remigius: Abiud is “He is my Father,” after “I and the Father are One” (John 10:30); Eliacim “God the Reviver”; Azor “aided”; Sadoch “the just,” after “the just for the unjust” (1 Peter 3:18); Achim “my brother is He”; Eliud “He is my God.” Raban runs the same names as a moral ascent, from the preparation of the Lord through prayer and the raising up from vices to the love of neighbour and of God. The Eastern Pseudo-Chrysostom supposes Jechonias, of whom nothing good or ill is written, to have besought God in the captivity for afflicted Israel, and reads Zorobabel as “the doctor of Babylon,” recalling how his sentence that Truth is strongest prevailed before Darius — “for what doctrine greater than to shew that Truth is the mistress of all things?”
16:
“And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.” The grammatical-historical commentators mark the deliberate change of formula. The long chain of “begat” breaks: not “Joseph begat Jesus,” but “Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom — of her — was born Jesus,” the Evangelist avoiding any word that would make him the natural father (cf. v.18). Chrysostom observes that, having gone through all the ancestry and ended in Joseph, he adds “the husband of Mary” to declare that it was for her sake he was included at all; and Gennadius draws the doctrinal consequence against Ebion, that the Son of God was born of human flesh, that is of Mary, “and not by man after the way of nature.”

The discrepancy with the third Gospel — Joseph son of Jacob here, son of Heli there — was already an objection in Jerome’s day, urged by the Emperor Julian. Jerome answers from the Hebrew usage that “one was his father by nature, the other by law,” and refers the reader to Africanus and Eusebius for the fuller treatment. That treatment Eusebius supplies: Matthan and Melchi, of one tribe but different race, had each a son by the same woman Jesca, Matthan begetting Jacob and Melchi afterwards begetting Heli, so that the two were brethren by their mother; and when Heli died childless, Jacob married his widow and begat Joseph, “by nature indeed his own son,” but by the law the son of Heli. Hence, Eusebius notes, the one Evangelist writes “begat” while the other carefully avoids the word to the end. Lightfoot and Wesley take a different road, holding that the one line is Mary’s and the other Joseph’s.

Augustine weighs the two and prefers nature here: Matthew’s steady phrase from Abraham down requires that Joseph was begotten, not adopted, by Jacob, while the other Evangelist, giving the ancestry not at the opening but at the baptism, “follows the line of adoption,” and so points out the Priest that should make atonement for sin — for by adoption we are made sons of God, whereas by the descent according to the flesh we see that the Son of God was for us made man. Augustine presses the same flesh against Valentinus, who taught that Christ took nothing of the Virgin but “passed through her as through a channel or pipe”; and he finds in this marriage every good of wedlock — progeny in the Lord himself, fidelity, and a sacrament, since there was neither adultery nor divorce. The line is brought down to Joseph, he adds, that no wrong be done the male sex in wedlock, “providing only nothing was taken away from the truth; because Mary was of the seed of David.”

Hilary explains the closing words: what the anointing with oil conveyed to kings, the Holy Spirit conveyed upon the man Christ, with expiation added, “wherefore when born He was called Christ.” Clarke and Calvin add that the title, answering the Hebrew Messiah, names his office as the appointed Redeemer. The Council of Ephesus warns against Nestorius, who would confine the names Christ, Son and Lord to the two natures severally; and Pseudo-Augustine against dividing the one who is “the same Christ the Son of both God and man.”
17:
“So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David until the carrying away into Babylon are fourteen generations; and from the carrying away into Babylon unto Christ are fourteen generations.” The witnesses note the Evangelist’s ordered division and discuss its purpose and difficulties. The grammatical-historical commentators take the arrangement as a memoria technica: Barnes and Ellicott observe that the three groups of fourteen were “for the purpose of aiding the memory,” a method “common among the Jews,” though “the periods embraced by the three groups were of very unequal length,” and names have been omitted to make the count even. Lightfoot notes the same threefold-fourteen pattern in the Jewish schools. Wesley points out the overlap by which the count is completed — David ends the first fourteen and begins the second, and Jesus ends the third.

The fathers find in the threefold division a deeper meaning. The Eastern Chrysostom and Pseudo-Chrysostom read it of the three changes in the people’s government — under patriarchs and judges, under kings, and after the captivity — “to show that not even by the change of their government were they made better,” but held “the same evil course” throughout. The Latin Remigius finds in fourteen (ten plus four) “the agreement of the Law”—the Decalogue—“and the Gospel”—the four books; Augustine accounts for the count by Jechonias being reckoned twice, at the turning-point of the captivity; the Gloss sees the “sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit” doubled for soul and body. The witnesses thus find in the verse both a practical and a theological design. Practically, the genealogy is shaped into three memorable epochs — the rise to David, the decline to the exile, the recovery to Christ — each of fourteen generations. Theologically, the division marks the unbroken faithfulness of God across every change of the nation’s fortunes: through patriarchs, kings, and exile alike, the line of promise ran its appointed course, until at the close of the third age the Christ was born, in whom the whole history of Israel reached its goal.

The witnesses draw the devotional lesson from the survey. To trace such a series of generations, through rise and fall and recovery, is to see the long patience of God working steadily toward one end. Each age had its changes, its faithful and its faithless, its glory and its shame; yet through all the promise held its course. The verse thus invites the reader to look back over the whole and adore the providence that, across two thousand years and forty-two generations, kept the line of David unbroken until the appointed time, when God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, to redeem his people.
18:
“Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost.” The witnesses note that the Evangelist deliberately breaks the chain of natural begettings to relate a birth like no other. The Eastern Chrysostom and Pseudo-Chrysostom mark that, having said “Jacob begat Joseph,” Matthew now “cuts off the thread,” announcing “some new thing,” lest any “suppose that Christ was born by the law” of nature. The grammatical-historical commentators supply the Jewish setting: Barnes, Clarke, and Lightfoot explain that “espoused” (betrothed) was a binding contract, after which the pair were already “husband” and “wife” though not yet come together, with an interval before the marriage. The decisive words are “of the Holy Ghost”: the child was conceived not by man but by the creative power of the Spirit (Ambrose — “Mary was with child of the Holy Spirit” by his power, not his substance).

The fathers guard both the virginity of the mother and the dignity of her Son. The Eastern Alexandrian voices defend the title “mother of God”: Origen calls Mary “the mother of God, of the Only-begotten,” and Cyril argues against Nestorius that she is not merely “the mother of Christ” but bears the One who is God. The Latin Jerome asks why Christ was conceived of a virgin espoused, and answers: that her family might be known through Joseph, that she might be shielded from the charge of adultery, and that she might have a protector. Augustine notes the wedlock was without carnal desire, befitting the sinless One. Henry, for the Puritan expositors, bids us adore the mystery, “not pry into it.” The witnesses thus find in the verse the foundation of the gospel — the virgin conception of the Son of God. The long genealogy has brought us to a birth that owes nothing to the will of man: Mary, a betrothed virgin, is found with child by the Holy Ghost, so that the Saviour, true man of her substance, is yet conceived without sin, the eternal Son entering our nature by a miracle of grace.
19:
“Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.” The witnesses dwell on Joseph’s character and the question his conduct raises. The grammatical-historical commentators render “just” (dikaios) as “upright,” a man of “Jewish conscientiousness” (Robertson; cf. Luke 1:6): he would neither marry one he supposed unfaithful nor expose her to “public infamy” (Clarke’s rendering of paradeigmatisai), but sought to “put her away privily,” quietly dissolving the betrothal. Lightfoot and Barnes find in this the meeting of justice and mercy — justice that could not overlook apparent sin, mercy that would not disgrace her.

The fathers debate how Joseph could be “just” if he meant to conceal what he took for sin. The Latin Jerome and Augustine answer that to spare her was itself a higher righteousness — “with great kindness” he would not betray what he alone knew (Augustine), and Ambrose praises him for keeping himself “guiltless of her blood, yet pure from her defilements.” But the Eastern Alexandrian Origen offers a striking alternative: Joseph “sought to put her away because he saw in her a great sacrament, to approach which he thought himself unworthy” — not suspecting sin at all, but withdrawing in reverent awe before the mystery. The witnesses thus find here both a portrait of godly character and a genuine debate. Most read Joseph as a righteous man caught in a painful dilemma, who, believing the worst, chose the gentlest course the law allowed — to release Mary without shame. Origen and a few read him as one who already sensed the holy thing in her and dared not claim her. Either way, the witnesses note the tenderness and integrity of the man God chose to guard his Son: just, yet merciful; troubled, yet unwilling to wound; and soon to be set at rest by the angel’s word.

The witnesses observe that, on every reading, Joseph stands as a model of quiet integrity. He neither rushed to condemn nor hardened his heart, but sought the way that was at once righteous and kind. The verse thus commends the spirit that, faced with another’s seeming fault, refuses both the cruelty of public exposure and the laxity of indifference, and waits, as Joseph waited, upon the will of God. His perplexity, honestly borne, was the soil in which the angel’s revelation could be received.
20:
“But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost.” The witnesses note the timely intervention and its tender address. The grammatical-historical commentators observe that Joseph “did not act hastily” (Barnes) but in his perplexity was met by the angel, who came “as the solution of his doubts” (Ellicott) in a dream — the recognised mode of divine communication. The angel calls him “son of David,” which the Eastern Pseudo-Chrysostom and the Gloss read as recalling “the promise of God to David, that of his seed should Christ be born,” and the “fear not” as banishing his distress.

The fathers and the Reformed draw out the doctrine and the comfort. Calvin, for the Reformed, marks how “seasonably the Lord aids his people,” showing that “when he appears not to observe our cares, we are still under his eye.” The Latin Augustine guards the truth against error: though the child is “of the Holy Ghost,” we may not say the Spirit is the “father” of the man Christ as God the Father begot the Word — “such an absurdity the ears of the faithful cannot bear” — for the Spirit is the agent, not the father, of the conception. Ambrose notes that calling Mary Joseph’s “wife” does not rob her of her virginity, the betrothed being so called by Scripture custom. The witnesses thus find in the verse the gracious resolving of Joseph’s anguish. At the very point of his deepest perplexity, God sends his angel to reveal the truth: Mary is no adulteress, but the chosen vessel of a miracle; the child is conceived by the Holy Ghost; and Joseph, far from putting her away, is to take her as his wife and guard the holy thing within her. The “son of David” is summoned to give the Son of God a place in the royal line, and his fear is turned to faith by the word from heaven.
21:
“And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.” The grammatical-historical commentators unfold the name. Jerome calls it a Hebrew word meaning Saviour, and points out that the etymology is supplied by the clause that follows; Gill and Barnes add that it answers to Joshua and to Hosea, from the verb that signifies to save, and Clarke traces the root yasha, he saved, delivered, put in a state of safety. Ellicott sketches its history: in its older form it meant “Jehovah is salvation,” and the change of the name of the captain of Israel from Hoshea to the fuller form that took in the divine name (Numbers 13:16) had made it “the expression of the deepest faith of the people,” while after the return it gained new prominence in the high priest Jeshua the son of Josedech (Haggai 1:1). Ellicott observes too that nothing is strange in Joseph hearing it here for the first time, though it had already been given to Mary, since the customs of betrothal forbade communication between them.

The Eastern and Latin voices dwell on the manner of the announcement. Chrysostom notes that the angel confirms a word “beyond human thought, and the law of nature” by telling not only what is past but what is to come, and that he interprets the name as he gives it, “suggesting good hope” — for we yield our belief more readily to good fortune. Pseudo-Chrysostom presses the wording: not “shall bear thee a son,” as was said to Zacharias of Elisabeth, for she who had not conceived of man bore the child not to her husband but to herself. Raban marks the verb — “thou shalt call,” not “shalt give him a name,” since the name “had been given from all eternity.” The Gloss adds a comfort to Joseph: though no need of him had been in the conception, there was need of his guardianship, to screen the mother from disgrace and to bring up and circumcise the child, at whose circumcision the naming would fall.

What the saving is, the commentators take pains to bound. Remigius: he saves “not the unbelieving, but his people; that is, those that believe on him,” and “not so much from visible as from invisible enemies… not by fighting with arms, but by remitting their sins.” Chrysologus turns the clause into an argument for the child’s deity — let those who ask who it is that Mary bore hear that he forgives sins, which even the unbelieving grant that God alone can do. Barnes draws the practical edge: the design was “not to save men IN their sins, but FROM their sins,” by atonement and by the renewing of the heart, so that no profession without deliverance from sin’s dominion is evidence of belonging to him. Clarke says the same of the whole dispensation: its perfection “is not that it makes allowances for sin, but that it makes an atonement for it: not that it tolerates sin, but that it destroys it.”
22:
“Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying…” The witnesses note the Evangelist’s own comment, marking the birth as the fulfilment of prophecy. The grammatical-historical commentators observe that this is “the custom of the Evangelist to confirm what he says out of the Old Testament” (Remigius), for the sake of Jewish believers, “that they might recognize as fulfilled in the grace of the Gospel the things foretold.” Robertson discusses the phrase “that it might be fulfilled” (hina plērōthē): the older grammarians (Alford) took it strictly as “in order that,” though modern grammarians recognise a looser use; the point, Ellicott adds, is the correspondence the Evangelist “could not possibly regard… as accidental.” Barnes supplies the context of the prophecy (Isaiah 7:14), delivered to Ahaz some 740 years before.

The fathers find in the formula the testimony of the whole Old Testament to Christ. The Eastern Chrysostom hears the angel comprising in this saying “the depths of the Divine mercy, the laws of nature broken through, and reconciliation made — He who was above all made lower than all.” Calvin, for the Reformed, warns against trifling that confines the prophecy to the bare name; it includes “whatever is heavenly and divine” in Christ. The witnesses thus find in the verse the Evangelist’s key for reading the nativity: it is no isolated marvel but the fulfilment of the prophetic word, the long-promised sign now given. Matthew pauses his narrative to point the believing reader back to Isaiah, that he may see in the virgin’s child the very thing the LORD had foretold to the house of David in the dark days of Ahaz. The witnesses note how this sets the pattern for the whole Gospel, which again and again shows the events of Christ’s life answering to the Scriptures — so that the faith of the Jew, and of every reader, might rest on the harmony of promise and fulfilment, the God of the prophets keeping his word in the birth of his Son.

The witnesses note how this verse shapes the reader’s whole approach to the Gospel. Matthew will not let the nativity be seen as a bare wonder, but ties it at once to the prophetic word, teaching that the God who acts in Christ is the God who spoke through the prophets. The verse thus binds the two Testaments together, and assures the believer that the coming of the Saviour was no afterthought but the keeping of an ancient promise, written centuries before in the dark days of Ahaz and now fulfilled to the letter.
23:
“Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.” The grammatical-historical commentators first fix the prophecy on Christ. Gill and Lightfoot hold that the words of Isaiah 7:14 can be understood “of no other” — not of Ahaz’s wife, nor of Hezekiah, who was already born. Clarke sets the scene that makes the oracle intelligible: Judah under Ahaz was brought very low, Pekah having slain a hundred and twenty thousand in one day and carried off two hundred thousand captives, while Rezin of Syria, confederate with him, had taken Elath and led its people away to Damascus; and when the king, “swallowed up now both by sorrow and by unbelief,” refused to ask a sign, the Lord gave one unasked. Jerome insists that a sign so given “ought to be something new and wonderful,” not the ordinary birth of a young woman. Ellicott grants the difficulty of tracing the Evangelist’s sense in the literal Hebrew, and Wesley explains the idiom by which “they shall call his name” means “he shall really and effectually be what he is called.”

The disputed word carries the weight of the argument, and Clarke defends it at length. Against the claim that almah need mean no more than a young married woman, he denies that the one text alleged for it (Proverbs 30:19) will bear the sense, and notes that the older versions read otherwise. He then rejects the usual etymology — that maidens were so called because kept concealed at home — as “purely fanciful,” since Rebecca, Rachel, Miriam and Ruth are all shown drawing water, keeping sheep and gleaning in the fields; the concealment intended is physical, that as a woman she had not been uncovered. This, he says, is the very force of the virgin’s own question, how this should be, seeing she knew no man (Luke 1:34), and it answers to the ancient word about the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15), which must come from the woman alone. To the objection that a birth centuries off could be no sign to Ahaz, he replies that the promise secured the city and the house of David until that birth — a point Lightfoot makes as a double comfort, of the deliverance then at hand and of the Christ to be born long after.

On the name itself the witnesses press the doctrine. Clarke renders it literally “the Strong God with Us,” and takes it of God incarnate, in the sense of the Word made flesh who dwelt among us (John 1:14) and of God manifested in the flesh (1 Timothy 3:16); the eating of butter and honey in the prophet marks him truly man, nourished in a natural way. Theodotus, against Photinus, presses that the child “now born” is no “mere man” but God. Calvin, for the Reformed, distinguishes the manner: the name teaches how God is with us — not merely by power and aid, as he is elsewhere, but in the person of the incarnate Son, who took our flesh to dwell in it.
24:
“Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife.” The witnesses note Joseph’s prompt and exact obedience. The grammatical-historical commentators observe that he “promptly obeyed the angel” (Robertson), and that “took unto him his wife” (parelaben tēn gynaika) means he took her home, completing the marriage — Ellicott noting the words “cover a great deal,” the formal ratification of the betrothal, the benediction, the marriage-feast, and the bringing of Mary into his house. Calvin, for the Reformed, finds in “the ready performance” a proof “of the certainty of Joseph’s faith” as well as “his obedience,” for had any scruple remained he “would not have moved a step.”

The fathers draw the lesson of obedience. The Gloss notes that Joseph “not only did what the angel commanded, but as he commanded it,” and bids every one warned of God “break off all delays, rise from sleep, and do that which is commanded.” The Latin Remigius sets Joseph’s obedience against Adam’s disobedience: “by Adam’s disobedience we were ruined; by Joseph’s obedience we all begin to be recalled to our former condition.” The witnesses thus find in the verse a model of faith expressed in action. Joseph, his doubts resolved by the angel’s word, does not delay or question but immediately does as he was bidden, taking Mary as his wife and so accepting the charge of guarding the Saviour and his mother. The witnesses note the quiet greatness of this obedience — that on it, humanly speaking, hung the sheltering of the Christ-child and the honour of his mother — and they commend in Joseph the pattern of every believer: to hear the word of God and at once obey it, without delay or reserve, trusting the One who speaks. His ready faith stands in honoured contrast to the world’s slowness, and shares, the fathers say, in the great reversal by which obedience undoes the ruin that disobedience wrought.

The witnesses press the contrast between Joseph’s ready obedience and the world’s delay. He rose at once and did all that was commanded, asking nothing for himself, content to serve the purpose of God in quiet faithfulness. The verse thus holds up a pattern for every believer: to receive the word of God not with argument or postponement but with immediate, glad obedience. In Joseph’s prompt rising the church has long seen the beauty of a faith that simply does what its Lord commands, and so becomes the guardian of the holy charge entrusted to it.
25:
“And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS.” The witnesses note the chaste reserve of Joseph and the long-debated question of Mary’s later children. The grammatical-historical commentators explain “knew her not” as a modest euphemism (Gill) for marital union, the imperfect tense marking that “Joseph lived in continence with Mary till the birth of Jesus” (Robertson). Two points have stirred controversy: the word “firstborn” (which Ellicott and Robertson note is absent from the best manuscripts) and the word “till.” On these turns the question whether Mary had other children afterward.

Here the witnesses divide along confessional lines. The Latin Jerome, against Helvidius, defends Mary’s perpetual virginity, holding that “till” and “firstborn” do not imply she bore other children. The grammatical-historical and Reformed commentators are more cautious: Barnes holds “the doctrine of the virginity of Mary before the birth of Jesus” to be scriptural and important, “but the Scriptures do not affirm that she had no children afterwards”; Clarke thinks one “may reasonably and piously believe” she had others. Wesley and Calvin agree, however, that the language does not settle it — Wesley citing that “Michal had no child till the day of her death” (2 Samuel 6:23), where “till” plainly implies nothing after; so “knew her not till” need not mean he knew her afterward. The witnesses thus find in the verse a clear affirmation and a contested inference. The clear affirmation is the virgin birth: Joseph did not know Mary until Jesus was born, so that the conception was wholly of the Holy Ghost, no human father sharing in it. The contested inference — whether Mary remained ever-virgin or bore Joseph children later — the witnesses leave where Scripture leaves it, agreeing that the text neither requires nor forbids the perpetual virginity, and that the great matter is the supernatural birth of the Saviour, to whom Joseph, in obedience, gave the appointed name, JESUS.

The witnesses agree that, whatever be concluded about Mary’s later life, the verse fixes beyond doubt the one thing needful — that the conception of Jesus owed nothing to man. Joseph’s continence guards the miracle: the child is wholly of the Holy Ghost. And the chapter closes as it has run, in obedience, as Joseph gives the babe the name the angel appointed. The genealogy of kings ends not in another begetting but in a Saviour named Jesus, born of a virgin, God with us, come to save his people from their sins.
